Now I have the full picture. Here's where the inconsistencies are.
The core flag, kHardwareVideoDecodeOnly, is now dead code. You flipped it to false at line 72, so the one guarded block that still checks it (if (kHardwareVideoDecodeOnly && config.IsVideo()) at line 447, inside CreateDecoder) is now a no-op. But the two new "HW-ONLY POLICY" blocks you added — in SupportsMimeType and Supports — don't check the flag at all, they're unconditional. So you've got one mechanism turned off and a second, newer mechanism hard-wired on. That's the main inconsistency: the toggle exists but no longer actually toggles anything.
SupportsMimeType is broader than Supports. The first blocks any video/* MIME type that isn't H.264. The second only blocks when MP4Decoder::IsH264 fails, but doesn't check the MIME prefix first — it relies on mConfig.IsVideo(). These should be equivalent in practice (audio configs skip the check either way), but the asymmetry in how the gate is expressed (string-prefix check vs. config-type check) means if IsVideo() and a video/-prefixed MIME type can ever diverge (e.g., a container reporting itself oddly), the two functions will disagree on whether to allow it.
PDMFactory.cpp line 922 has a third "PATCH: Hardware-only gate" comment — let me check that one too, since it wasn't in the diff output above (the diff only showed line-range changes near the top of the file). View context around line 922 patch
Good — that's a third copy of the same gate (this one is the static, remote-process variant). Now I have everything I need to give you a real answer.
Across the three files, your stated goal — block all non-H.264 software video decoding, force hardware-only H.264 — is implemented redundantly and inconsistently rather than from one source of truth. Specifically:
1. The kill switch doesn't kill anything anymore. kHardwareVideoDecodeOnly flipped from true to false (PDMFactory.cpp:72), and the one place that still respects it (CreateDecoder, line 447) is now effectively disabled. But you separately hard-coded the same restriction, unconditionally, in Supports() and SupportsMimeType(). If the intent was "make this a single toggleable feature," it's not — half the gate is permanently on regardless of the flag, and half is permanently off. If the intent was "always hard-lock, remove the toggle," then the dead flag and dead if block at line 447 should be deleted, not left as inert clutter.
2. The four gates use different predicates for "is this allowed."
PDMFactory::Supports (instance method, line 487-490): allows only if MP4Decoder::IsH264. PDMFactory::SupportsMimeType (instance method, line 471-474): allows only if MP4Decoder::IsH264, gated on StringBeginsWith(aMimeType, "video/"). PDMFactory::SupportsMimeType (static, remote-process variant, line ~922): allows if IsH264, otherwise blocks video/* prefix or explicitly VP8/VP9/AV1/HEVC — a belt-and-suspenders check that's redundant with the prefix check but at least explicit. DecoderTraits::CanHandleCodecsType (DecoderTraits.cpp): blocks based on substring matches in the codec string ("av01", "vp9", "vp09", "vp8", "hev1", "hvc1") plus blocking video/webm, video/x-webm, video/ogg MIME types outright — a completely different detection strategy (string search on the raw original type string) than the other three (typed MIME/codec checks via MP4Decoder::IsH264 etc).
That last one is the riskiest inconsistency: aType.OriginalString().Find("vp9") is a raw substring search over whatever string was passed in, not a parsed codec check. It will misfire on coincidental substrings (anything with "vp9" or "vp8" appearing inside a filename-like or parameter-like portion of the type string) and won't catch codec strings that don't literally contain those substrings but still mean VP9/AV1/HEVC. The PDMFactory versions are more rigorous, using VPXDecoder::IsVP8/IsVP9, AOMDecoder::IsAV1, MP4Decoder::IsHEVC. DecoderTraits should be using the same typed helpers instead of string-searching, both for correctness and so the four gates can't drift further out of sync.
3. CanHandleMediaType (DecoderTraits.cpp, container-only branch) blocks Ogg/WebM but not Matroska, even though MatroskaDecoder::IsSupportedType later in the same function still returns CANPLAY_MAYBE. If the policy is "no software-decoded containers without codec info," Matroska (which routes to VP9/AV1/etc. just as often as WebM) is a gap — it falls through unblocked while WebM is blocked at the same chokepoint.
4. RemoteVideoDecoder.cpp is identical to its .orig. Despite containing a "PATCH: Zero-copy IPC enforcement" comment, that's not something you added — the diff against the .orig file is empty, meaning this enforcement is either pre-existing/unrelated to your hardware-only effort, or you intended to make a change here that never landed. If your hardware-only policy was also supposed to touch the remote decoder's frame handling, that change is missing.
Net effect: you have at least four independent enforcement points for the same rule, expressed three different ways (typed codec check, MIME-prefix check, raw substring search on the original type string), one disabled toggle still wired into dead code, and one container format (Matroska) that slipped through the container-level gate. If this is meant to be a single coherent policy rather than defense-in-depth, I'd consolidate it into one shared predicate (e.g., a static bool IsHardwareOnlyAllowed(mimeType, codecString) helper using the typed MP4Decoder/VPXDecoder/AOMDecoder checks) and call that from all four sites, then delete the dead kHardwareVideoDecodeOnly flag and its now-unreachable branch — or restore it as the actual single toggle if you want this to remain switchable.

I need to stop you here before going further, because the hardware context you just gave actually contradicts the strategy in the patches, and proceeding would make your laptop worse at the thing you want, not better.
The HD 4000 in your i7-3632QM cannot decode VP9, AV1, or HEVC in hardware. Period. Intel Quick Sync on Ivy Bridge (HD 4000, GT2) only has fixed-function decode for H.264, MPEG-2, and VC-1. VP9 hardware decode didn't arrive in Intel iGPUs until Skylake/Kaby Lake-ish generations (and even then partially), AV1 not until Gen11/Tiger Lake, and HEVC decode arrived with Broadwell. Ivy Bridge predates all three. So "reject everything that isn't H.264 so the ASIC handles it" is correct only for H.264 — for VP9/AV1/HEVC there is no ASIC path on this chip to fall back to. Your patches don't add a hardware path for those codecs; they just return CANPLAY_NO / empty DecodeSupportSet, which means the browser won't play that content at all — not "decode it in hardware instead," just refuses it outright.
That changes what the patches actually do versus what you described. Let's separate the two real effects:
What the patches correctly achieve: for H.264, VPXDecoder/AOM checks gate everything else off, so H.264 (which HD 4000 does decode via Quick Sync) is the only video path left standing. That part is sound for this hardware, assuming the existing GetDecoderModule/PDM machinery actually routes H.264 through the platform decoder module (WMF on Windows, VA-API on Linux) rather than ffmpeg's software path — that's a separate wiring question from the gating logic, and the gating alone doesn't guarantee it.
What they actually do for VP9/AV1/WebM/Ogg/Matroska: hard rejection, full stop. Not "software-decode is forbidden so use hardware instead" — there is no hardware, so the content simply won't play. If a site serves you a WebM/VP9 stream with no H.264 fallback (increasingly common — YouTube defaults to VP9/AV1 for many resolutions), you'll get nothing instead of a slow-but-working software decode. Given a Turks dGPU that's disabled in BIOS and a 4-core/8-thread 35W Ivy Bridge part, "we have a perfectly good ASIC" is true only for H.264; for everything else the honest tradeoff is CPU load vs. no video at all, not CPU load vs. ASIC.
I'd like to know which tradeoff you actually want before I touch the source, since the current patch set picks "no video" silently and that's worth confirming deliberately rather than by default.
Q: For codecs the HD 4000 has no hardware decode for (VP9, AV1, HEVC, and WebM/Ogg containers) — what should happen? A: Hard block them (current behavior): browser refuses to play, no CPU fallback ever
Q: Should I also fix the actual H.264 hardware routing (PDM/VA-API wiring) so H.264 reliably goes through Quick Sync rather than just gating other codecs off? A: Yes, check and fix the H.264 hardware decode path too
Q: Want me to also fix the inconsistencies I flagged (dead flag, duplicated/divergent logic across 4 call sites, Matroska gap, fragile substring matching)? A: Yes, consolidate into one shared, consistent policy 22:29
